CausalChain: CLDN18.2 overexpression on gastric cancer cells -> Acidic and hypoxic tumor microenvironment impairs immune function -> Conventional CLDN18.2-targeted CAR-T cells show limited persistence and cytotoxicity -> Enhanced glycolytic capacity (via upregulation of HK2/PFK1) improves energy production under stress -> Concurrent checkpoint knockdown and chemokine receptor expression further improve survival and trafficking -> Multifunctional CAR-T cells maintain function and persist -> Enhanced tumor cell lysis and therapeutic outcomes.
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that engineering multifunctional CLDN18.2-specific CAR-T cells—by integrating enhanced glycolytic capacity through upregulation of key enzymes (HK2, PFK1), CRISPR-based knockdown of inhibitory checkpoints (e.g., PD-1, Tim-3), and the expression of chemokine receptor CCR6—will overcome the deleterious effects of the acidic and hypoxic tumor microenvironment in gastric cancer. These modifications are expected to increase energy production under stress, improve cellular persistence, promote effective trafficking into tumor sites, and bolster cytotoxic activity, thus resulting in superior tumor cell lysis and overall therapeutic efficacy.
Abstract: Gastric cancer is characterized by the overexpression of CLDN18.2 and a harsh, acidic, and hypoxic tumor microenvironment that impairs immune cell function. In this study, we propose the engineering of multifunctional CLDN18.2-specific CAR-T cells that incorporate metabolic reprogramming by upregulating key glycolytic enzymes (e.g., HK2, PFK1) alongside targeted knockdown of inhibitory receptors (e.g., PD-1, Tim-3) and expression of chemokine receptor CCR6 to enhance tumor trafficking. By leveraging state-of-the-art CRISPR-based gene editing, metabolic flux analysis, and microfluidic systems to mimic the tumor milieu, these CAR-T cells are designed to overcome acid-induced energy deficits, maintain persistence, improve cytotoxic activity, and ultimately enhance tumor cell lysis. This integrative approach builds upon the original hypothesis by addressing metabolic, immunosuppressive, and trafficking limitations in a comprehensive manner, offering a robust therapeutic strategy for gastric cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on enhancing glycolytic capacity to improve CAR-T cell persistence and cytotoxicity in an acidic TME. The revised hypothesis builds directly on this causal chain by: (1) specifying the upregulation of key glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFK1) to mechanistically boost energy production under acidic and hypoxic conditions; (2) incorporating the knockdown of inhibitory checkpoint molecules to further relieve immunosuppressive signaling; and (3) adding chemokine receptor expression (CCR6) to enhance tumor trafficking. Additionally, the new hypothesis leverages advanced gene editing and metabolic monitoring technologies to refine and test the approach, thereby addressing multiple dimensions of the tumor microenvironment and ensuring improved therapeutic outcomes.
